Baker v. Carr. The 1962 Supreme Court decision that held federal courts could review legislative apportionment and reapportionment cases, overturning the political question doctrine that had barred judicial intervention. Tennessee had not reapportioned its state legislative districts since 1901, despite massive population shifts. Urban voters were vastly underrepresented. Charles Baker challenged the apportionment as unconstitutional, but courts initially dismissed the case as a nonjusticiable political question.

Justice William Brennan wrote the majority opinion, holding that apportionment disputes are justiciable under the Equal Protection Clause, not barred as political questions. The decision removed the longstanding doctrine that courts cannot intervene in disputes over how legislatures are structured. This was a revolutionary shift. It opened the floodgates to reapportionment litigation. Within a year, federal courts were ordering redistricting in multiple states. The decision led directly to Reynolds v. Sims in 1964, which established the one person, one vote standard for state legislative apportionment. Baker v. Carr fundamentally altered the separation of powers and the justiciability doctrine itself.
